title: A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature

concept.text: The innovation would be a physical three-dimensional material or engineered lattice that protects one encoded quantum bit against thermal noise without repeated measurements or corrective feedback during storage. Below a fixed nonzero operating temperature, larger samples would retain recoverable quantum information for progressively longer times. Protecting a qubit requires preserving arbitrary quantum superpositions, so the system must suppress both bit-flip and phase-flip errors rather than merely preserve a classical binary state.

Passive storage does not require every stage of operation to be passive. External control may prepare the encoded state and recover it at the end; the defining capability is protection during the intervening storage interval. The relevant theoretical picture combines a chosen logical state with thermal syndrome degrees of freedom. It concerns long but finite retention of recoverable information, not permanent storage of an arbitrary qubit in the fully thermalized, infinite-time Gibbs state.

The laboratory innovation remains distinct from its mathematical starting point. The supplied May 2026 construction describes a local three-dimensional Hamiltonian encoding one logical qubit. Turning such a construction into a fabricated, controllable system with verified thermal protection is the intended advance. Universal gates and room-temperature operation would extend that achievement but are not required to establish passive storage at a laboratory-accessible nonzero temperature.

significance.text: If realized and validated, this would establish a major new way to protect quantum information: the system's interactions and thermal dynamics would provide protection throughout storage without an external correction cycle. Its direct consequence would be a laboratory memory whose recoverable quantum lifetime improves with system size at a fixed nonzero temperature. That would connect quantum information protection to the collective behavior of a physical many-body system.

A possible downstream benefit would be less measurement, decoding, and feedback activity while quantum information is idle. Whether that translates into lower total resource use would depend on fabrication costs, operating temperature, preparation and recovery complexity, and achievable storage fidelity. Passive protection also need not replace active correction everywhere: a useful architecture could combine a passive memory with actively controlled processing. These are conditional architectural possibilities, not demonstrated consequences of the supplied construction.

The analogy to a stable phase of matter has limits. A lifetime that grows rapidly with size does not by itself establish that the construction belongs to a distinct new thermal phase; the source leaves its relationship to known phases open. Nor does long-lived thermal encoding imply indefinite equilibrium retention: the source states that the input logical information becomes unrecoverable at infinite time after full thermalization.

A passive memory would not automatically be a universal quantum computer. The source identifies fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates through code switching while coupled to a thermal bath as a further bottleneck. Room-temperature storage likewise requires suitable physical interaction energy scales and verified stability at that temperature. A nonzero theoretical critical temperature alone supplies neither a kelvin-valued operating point nor evidence that ambient operation is feasible.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an experimentally realized, local three-dimensional system that protects both quantum error types for increasingly long times at a fixed accessible temperature. The supplied preprint explains the obstruction in two-dimensional stabilizer memories through string-like operators that create point-like excitations, which thermally proliferate. Within that setting, increasing system size does not yield a lifetime that keeps growing at fixed nonzero temperature. A successful three-dimensional design must prevent thermal processes from destroying either component of the encoded quantum information.

A concrete engineering barrier is implementing the mathematical Hamiltonian as physical interactions while preserving its relevant locality and protection mechanisms. An experiment must also show that its environment produces sufficiently favorable thermal dynamics: the theoretical lifetime claim assumes specified local Markovian thermalization, and an actual device may experience additional noise channels. Proposed practical requirements include bounded interaction strengths and ranges as the lattice grows, an accessible operating temperature, and enough control to initialize and recover the encoded qubit. These requirements are a synthesis of what would make the laboratory claim interpretable, not achievements reported in the supplied evidence.

Robustness remains a separate scientific obstacle. In the supplied version, the authors defer a TQO-2 argument needed for their proposed spectral-gap stability reasoning. Even establishing spectral-gap stability would not, by itself, demonstrate that the thermal memory lifetime retains its scaling under realistic coupling perturbations. The explicit-embedding variant also has a deferred complete lifetime proof. These gaps must be distinguished from the separate lifetime claim made for the random-embedding construction.

Efficient preparation and usable final recovery are additional practical barriers. The source explicitly leaves efficient passive initialization unaddressed. Controlled initialization is compatible with the storage concept, but a useful laboratory memory still needs a preparation procedure, a recovery procedure, and evidence that their errors do not overwhelm the protection gained during storage.

current_state.text: The supplied source is Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, and Ting-Chun Lin's “A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions,” arXiv version 1, dated May 11, 2026. It claims a three-dimensional Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonian encoding one logical qubit, with geometric locality and a memory-lifetime lower bound exponential in a positive power of the physical qubit count below a nonzero critical temperature, under specified local thermalization dynamics. This is a theoretical construction, not a demonstrated material or device.

The scaling variable matters. An exponential in a positive power of qubit count does not establish an exponential specifically in linear sample size without the exponent and the relationship between qubit count and geometry. The supplied informal theorems also give no critical temperature in kelvin. Their positive-temperature claim therefore does not establish a particular laboratory operating temperature, much less room-temperature performance.

The supplied text identifies unfinished work: the TQO-2 prerequisite for the proposed perturbative-stability argument is deferred to an updated version, and the complete exponential-lifetime proof for the explicit-embedding variant is left to future work. The latter limitation concerns that variant and should not be read as a retraction of the separate random-embedding lifetime claim. Robust thermal-lifetime scaling under perturbations is not established by the inspected passages.

The supplied review verified the source's identity, but the retained extraction is limited to 120,000 characters and ends during Section 3.2.3, before the main lifetime proof. Consequently, the review could assess the stated results and documented qualifications but could not inspect the complete proof. This access limitation does not show that the theoretical result is false.

The supplied materials contain no freshness-search record establishing developments through November 1, 2026. They therefore do not determine whether a later version resolved these gaps, whether peer-reviewed publication followed, whether this remains the strongest theoretical result, or whether subsequent experimental realizations exist. The supplied source itself reports a theoretical construction; it does not establish the absence of material, cold-atom, or superconducting-circuit implementations elsewhere. No evidence was supplied to substantiate the earlier Willow and Helios comparisons.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: fabricate a family of local three-dimensional lattices and store arbitrary encoded qubit states without active feedback during a clearly defined storage interval. Use controlled initialization and final recovery as needed. At a fixed measured nonzero temperature, well above the apparatus base temperature by a stated experimental margin, measure recovery fidelity after increasing storage times and define the memory lifetime using an explicit fidelity threshold. The temperature margin and fidelity threshold are proposed experimental choices, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Encoded qubit lifetime without feedback at fixed nonzero temperature

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scaling test: keep physical interaction strengths and ranges bounded independently of system size, define linear size precisely, and demonstrate lifetimes consistent with exponential growth in that size across a sufficiently broad family of devices. This is deliberately stronger and more specific than the supplied theorem's exponential dependence on a positive power of qubit count. Analysis should compare plausible alternative scaling laws and account for preparation, recovery, and measurement uncertainty. A finite collection of sizes establishes observed scaling over that range, not an asymptotic law by itself.
completion_criteria.label: Lifetimes consistent with exponential growth in linear size, interactions bounded

completion_criteria.text: Proposed robustness and reproducibility tests: vary couplings within a stated range, quantify relevant environmental noise, and show that the claimed lifetime advantage survives those changes. Repeat the result across independently prepared samples and, ideally, independent laboratories. Recovery tests should probe both bit-flip and phase-flip protection, including superpositions or entanglement with a reference, so that classical-state retention cannot masquerade as quantum storage. Finite tests establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality over all states, perturbations, or environments.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduced bit-flip and phase-flip lifetime advantage under perturbations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report the operating-temperature range, interaction scales, device sizes, initialization and recovery costs, and maximum measured retention time. Universal gates, efficient passive initialization, and room-temperature operation would be valuable extensions but are not required for this memory claim. Indefinite storage is not the proposed test; even convincing exponential scaling concerns recoverable information over finite times.
completion_criteria.label: Report operating conditions, resource costs, and maximum retention time

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” and QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls,” share the goal of reliable quantum information but target computational capabilities beyond storage. QUA-04 could supply a memory component without establishing universal gates, a scalable computational architecture, or bounded computational overhead. Conversely, success on either computational concept would not by itself demonstrate passive thermal storage.

Roster-based comparison: QUA-05, “Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons,” also connects quantum information protection to many-body physics, but its defining capability is universal computation through braiding. QUA-04 asks for passive thermal retention in a three-dimensional material. Neither the supplied roster nor the reviewed construction establishes that these mechanisms coincide.

Roster-based comparison: QUA-06, “Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules,” concerns reliable communication between modules. A passive memory might help retain states while communication proceeds, but it does not establish a fault-tolerant interconnect. QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator,” shares an interest in practical hardware and operating conditions. Its title specifies a manufacturing and computational goal that differs from passive storage at nonzero temperature; it supplies no basis for asserting a particular correction mechanism or room-temperature operation.

Roster-based comparison: QUA-02, “Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm,” QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” and QUA-09, “An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data,” concern successful computational tasks. Passive storage could become an enabling component, but it would not establish the required algorithms, processing scale, prediction accuracy, data handling, or speedup in any of these entries.

Roster-based comparison: QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems,” is a mathematical complexity separation. Building a passive quantum memory would demonstrate a physical information-storage capability, not prove that separation. All of these entries retain distinct completion conditions even where a future architecture might combine their capabilities.

brief.title: Quantum memory that protects itself during storage
possible: You could leave a quantum bit—a unit of information that can combine states—in a laboratory memory without continual checks or corrective feedback. At a fixed temperature above absolute zero, a larger memory would keep that information recoverable for longer.
why: For quantum-computer builders, the memory's own interactions would protect stored information. This would reduce measurement and feedback activity while information sits idle, allowing passive storage to work alongside actively controlled processing.

sources.who: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova and Ting-Chun Lin
sources.showed: Their preprint presents a mathematical design for a three-dimensional quantum memory. Under specified thermal noise, its storage lifetime grows rapidly with the number of components.
sources.quote: We construct a 3D Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonian whose ground state space can encode a qubit for exponential time when coupled to a bath at non-zero temperature.
sources.cited_for: A theoretical route to passive quantum storage using interactions between nearby components.
sources.not_established: A working device and lifetime scaling that survives realistic imperfections remain to be demonstrated.

sources.who: Yifan Hong, Jinkang Guo and Andrew Lucas
sources.showed: They showed theoretically that certain quantum error-correcting designs can protect information through thermal dynamics without a thermodynamic phase transition—a collective change in a material's equilibrium behavior.
sources.quote:
Slow Gibbs
sampling of such codes enables fault-tolerant passive quantum error correction using finite-depth
circuits.
sources.cited_for: Passive quantum protection need not depend on an equilibrium phase transition.
sources.not_established: The designs allow interactions over unrestricted distances, so they do not establish a memory built from nearby interactions in ordinary space.

shown: Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin have proposed a mathematical memory whose predicted lifetime improves rapidly as it grows, below a nonzero temperature threshold. Their preprint provides a theoretical starting point; a fabricated memory with this behavior remains the target.
missing: A physical lattice must preserve quantum combinations of states for longer as it grows, at a fixed accessible temperature without feedback during storage.
Real interactions and environmental noise must preserve the predicted lifetime advantage despite imperfections.
Preparation and final recovery must work well enough that their errors do not overwhelm the protection gained during storage.

milestones.label: Quantum storage without feedback at a fixed nonzero temperature
milestones.explanation: A family of three-dimensional lattices would have to retain arbitrary quantum states above the apparatus's minimum temperature, using a stated recovery-quality threshold. This would establish passive storage under measured conditions.

milestones.label: Lifetimes grow exponentially with length while interactions stay bounded
milestones.explanation: Across a broad size range, lifetimes would have to multiply with each equal increase in length while interaction strengths and ranges stay bounded. This would establish the required size advantage over competing growth patterns.

milestones.label: Both quantum protections survive imperfections and repeated experiments
milestones.explanation: Repeated tests would have to protect against value flips and changes in how combined states relate, despite varied couplings and environmental noise. This would distinguish robust quantum storage from retention of ordinary bits.

milestones.label: Operating conditions, costs and longest retention time are reported
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to report temperature range, interaction strengths, device sizes, preparation and recovery costs, and longest measured retention. This would define the memory's practical operating limits.

uncertain: How the predicted growth with component count translates into growth with physical length remains open.
The operating temperature and physical interaction strengths needed for a realizable device remain unknown.
Whether the lifetime advantage survives realistic imperfections and environmental dynamics remains unresolved.

page.title: Three-dimensional self-correcting quantum memory
page.definition: A fabricated three-dimensional lattice stores a logical qubit—a quantum bit encoded across physical components—through interactions with a thermal bath alone during storage. At a fixed temperature above absolute zero, arbitrary quantum states remain recoverable for times that grow without bound as lattice size increases.

goal.need: Active quantum storage requires encoding hardware and repeated operations that diagnose errors. Google Quantum AI's experiments quantify these resources in the table. NIST identifies additional qubits and measurements as sources of hardware overhead. Thermal self-correction seeks protection during storage through the system's interactions with its environment.

figures.caption: Resources used in Google Quantum AI's active quantum-memory experiments
figures.note: Distance is a code parameter governing error protection. The distance-7 and distance-5 results concern separate experiments; these figures do not measure the resources of a passive memory.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology, quoting Simon Lieu of JQI and QuICS
statements.quote: It usually requires that you build in additional qubits and make additional measurements to find the errors
statements.context: The passage concerns quantum error correction's hardware overhead. The proposed alternative discussed by NIST uses continuously driven photonic cavities, rather than thermal self-correction alone.

statements.body: Caltech–UC San Diego–Hon Hai Research Institute construction team: Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin
statements.quote: without the need for active error correction or other external sources of power.
statements.context: The authors describe their target of thermal self-correction. Their preprint of 11 May 2026 reports a mathematical construction, not a fabricated memory, and is not peer reviewed.

completion.title: A laboratory memory satisfies the published criteria for three-dimensional thermal self-correction.
completion.criterion: A fabricated family of three-dimensional local Hamiltonians encodes at least one qubit in a ground-state subspace whose energy splitting vanishes as size increases. Interaction range, strength and number of interactions per qubit remain bounded independently of size. At a fixed sufficiently low temperature T>0, recoverable quantum lifetime diverges with system size without active correction or powered stabilization during storage. Ground-space protection and thermal storage survive sufficiently weak local static perturbations. Final decoding runs in polynomial time; external control may prepare and recover the state.
completion.set_by: Landon-Cardinal, Yoshida, Poulin and Preskill, Physical Review A (2015), Introduction, definition (i)–(iii); Brown and colleagues, Reviews of Modern Physics (2016), Section III.G, criteria (1)–(5). These are published research conventions, not a certification standard.
completion.threshold_quote: a time which grows without bound as the system size increases
completion.basis: The published definitions distinguish self-correction from a fixed storage duration or improvement confined to small samples. Brown and colleagues additionally require bounded local interactions, perturbation robustness and efficient readout. The 2026 construction supplies an ideal-model lifetime bound, while leaving a prerequisite for its proposed gap-stability argument unproved and reporting no device.

milestones.title: A three-dimensional laboratory Hamiltonian encodes at least one qubit in its ground-state subspace.
milestones.criterion: Realize a three-dimensional local Hamiltonian with an encoded ground-state subspace of dimension at least two. Across a growing family, splitting within that subspace tends to zero, while interaction strengths, ranges and the number of interactions per component remain bounded. This establishes the physical encoding before thermal lifetime scaling is required. The preprint of 11 May 2026 establishes a one-qubit encoding and geometric locality mathematically; it reports no fabricated Hamiltonian.
milestones.set_by: Landon-Cardinal and colleagues, Physical Review A (2015), definition (i); Brown and colleagues, Reviews of Modern Physics (2016), Section III.G, criteria (1) and (3).
milestones.threshold_quote: the ground state is degenerate in the limit of a large system

milestones.title: A three-dimensional quantum memory permits final decoding in polynomial time after thermal errors.
milestones.criterion: Recover the encoded quantum information after thermal errors using a final decoder whose runtime is polynomial in physical-qubit count. External control is permitted at readout. Bravyi and Haah's preprint of 14 December 2011 supplies an efficient decoder for topological stabilizer codes, including the cubic-code model. This is an algorithmic result; it does not demonstrate decoding from a fabricated thermal memory.
milestones.set_by: Brown and colleagues, Reviews of Modern Physics (2016), Section III.G, criterion (5) and its preceding discussion of decoding runtime.

milestones.title: A three-dimensional thermal quantum memory retains a qubit longer as size increases over a finite range.
milestones.criterion: At a fixed nonzero bath temperature, a fabricated three-dimensional memory has recoverable qubit lifetimes that increase with size over a finite range, without powered stabilization or feedback during storage. Both bit and phase errors must be protected. Williamson's result published on 25 August 2026 establishes finite-cutoff exponential lifetime growth for layer codes mathematically. Hong, Guo and Lucas prove passive thermal storage for codes without three-dimensional geometric locality. Neither result is a fabricated memory.
milestones.set_by: Brown and colleagues, Reviews of Modern Physics (2016), Sections III.G and VII.A, distinguish finite-cutoff lifetime improvement, called partial self-correction, from full self-correction.
milestones.threshold_quote: coherence times that increase with system size up to some cutoff.

milestones.title: A three-dimensional memory's finite-size thermal protection survives weak local perturbations.
milestones.criterion: The fabricated memory's finite-size increase in recoverable quantum lifetime persists under sufficiently weak local perturbations of its interactions. This applies the published robustness requirement to the finite-size precursor; unbounded lifetime remains the completion test. The preprint of 11 May 2026 defers the TQO-2 condition needed for its proposed spectral-gap stability argument. It does not establish robustness of thermal lifetime scaling under perturbations.
milestones.set_by: Brown and colleagues, Reviews of Modern Physics (2016), Section III.G, criterion (4), with the preceding requirement covering arbitrary sufficiently weak local Hamiltonian perturbations.
milestones.threshold_quote: Memory properties are robust under local perturbations.

not_found: No regulator, standards body, government programme or prize rule specifying a finite laboratory certification test for three-dimensional thermal self-correction was found.
No published laboratory realization demonstrating size-dependent thermal protection of both logical error types in a three-dimensional local Hamiltonian was found.
No published numerical tolerance for the perturbation-robustness criterion or required number of experimental sizes was found.
